title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
abstract_summary: Language models (LMs) often struggle with basic functionality like arithmetic or factual lookup, despite their impressive zero-shot capabilities. This paper introduces Toolformer, a model trained to autonomously decide which external tools to call, when to call them, and how to use the results for token prediction. The training process is self-supervised, requiring only a handful of human-written demonstrations for each API. Toolformer incorporates tools such as a calculator, a Q&A system, a search engine, a translation system, and a calendar. The model achieves significantly improved zero-shot performance across various downstream tasks, often competing with much larger models. Importantly, it achieves these gains without sacrificing its core language modeling abilities.
problem_and_motivation: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive zero-shot and few-shot capabilities but suffer from inherent limitations that scaling alone cannot fully address. These include an inability to access up-to-date information, a tendency to hallucinate facts, difficulties with low-resource languages, a lack of precise mathematical skills, and an unawareness of the progression of time. Existing approaches to tool use either rely on large amounts of human-annotated data or are restricted to task-specific settings, hindering widespread adoption. There was a need for a model that can learn to use tools in a self-supervised, general-purpose manner without requiring extensive human supervision.
contributions: Introduction of Toolformer, a language model that learns to use external tools in a self-supervised way.
A novel method for generating and filtering API calls based on whether they reduce the model's perplexity on future tokens.
Demonstration that Toolformer can learn to control a variety of tools (QA, calculator, search, translation, calendar) without sacrificing core language modeling performance.
Empirical evidence showing Toolformer outperforms much larger models (like GPT-3 175B) on various zero-shot downstream tasks.
Provision of a framework that is agnostic to the dataset, allowing for tool-use learning on the same data used for pretraining.

method.overview: Toolformer is trained to use tools by augmenting a standard language modeling dataset with API calls. The process involves three main steps: 1) Sampling potential API calls using the model's in-context learning ability, 2) Executing these calls and filtering them based on whether they reduce the model's cross-entropy loss on future tokens, and 3) Finetuning the model on the augmented dataset. This allows the model to learn to decide when and how to use tools based on its own feedback, without requiring large-scale human annotations.

components.name: Sampling API Calls
components.description: For each API, a prompt is written to encourage the model to annotate text with API calls. The model computes the probability of starting an API call at each position in the text. Positions with a probability above a threshold are selected, and the model samples up to m API calls for each selected position.

components.name: Executing API Calls
components.description: The generated API calls are executed to obtain results. The execution mechanism depends on the tool (e.g., calling a neural network, executing a Python script, or using a retrieval system). The response must be a single text sequence.

components.name: Filtering API Calls
components.description: The model evaluates whether an API call is helpful by comparing the weighted cross-entropy loss with and without the tool's response. An API call is kept if the loss reduction exceeds a threshold, ensuring that the tool's output actually aids in predicting future tokens.
components.equations_or_algorithms: Li(z) = - sum(wj-i * log pM(xj | z, x1:j-1)); L-i - L+i >= tf

components.name: Model Finetuning
components.description: The filtered API calls are interleaved with the original text to create an augmented dataset. The model is then finetuned on this augmented dataset using a standard language modeling objective.

method.settings: The base model is GPT-J (6.7B parameters). Finetuning uses a batch size of 128, a learning rate of 1e-5, and linear warmup for the first 10% of training. Training is performed using DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 on 8 NVIDIA A100 40GB GPUs with BF16 precision.

tasks_and_datasets.name: LAMA (SQuAD, Google-RE, T-REx)
tasks_and_datasets.metric: Accuracy (lenient: correct word within first 5 predictions)

tasks_and_datasets.name: Multilingual QA (MLQA)
tasks_and_datasets.metric: Accuracy (percentage of generations containing the answer)

experiments.setup_details: All models evaluated in a zero-shot setting without providing in-context examples. Standard greedy decoding is used, with a modification for Toolformer to allow API calls if the <API> token is among the top k most likely tokens.

results.takeaway: Toolformer significantly outperforms all baselines, including much larger models.
Toolformer's use of the calculator tool leads to substantial performance gains, outperforming much larger models.
Toolformer outperforms GPT-J but still lags behind the much larger GPT-3.

claims_table.claim: Toolformer outperforms much larger models on LAMA.

ablations_and_analysis.finding: Increasing k (number of top tokens considered for API call) increases the frequency of API calls, leading to better performance on WebQS but potentially introducing noise.
Ability to use tools emerges at around 775M parameters. Larger models make better use of tools.
ablations_and_analysis.numbers: Figure 4 shows performance gap between Toolformer and Toolformer (disabled) increases with size.

limitations: Inability to use tools in a chain (output of one tool as input for another).
Lack of interactive tool use (e.g., browsing search results or refining queries).
Sensitivity to input wording when deciding whether to call an API.
Sample-inefficiency (requires processing millions of documents for a few thousand useful calls).
Does not account for tool-dependent computational costs when deciding to call an API.
failure_modes: Generating API calls that do not provide useful information.
Getting stuck in loops if not restricted to one API call per input.
Sensitivity to prompt wording leading to inconsistent tool usage.
future_work: Iteratively applying the approach to improve sample efficiency.
Incorporating computational cost into the decision-making process for API calls.
Improving search engine interaction (e.g., query reformulation).

key_claims.claim: LMs can teach themselves to use external tools in a self-supervised way.
Toolformer achieves competitive performance with much larger models without sacrificing core language modeling abilities.

definitions_and_terms.meaning: A language model finetuned to autonomously decide when and how to use external tools via API calls.
A training approach where the model learns to use tools by filtering API calls based on their ability to reduce perplexity on future tokens.

related_work_positioning: The paper positions Toolformer against existing tool-use approaches that rely on large amounts of human supervision (e.g., Komeili et al., 2022; Thoppilan et al., 2022) or are limited to task-specific settings (e.g., Gao et al., 2022; Parisi et al., 2022). It is most closely related to TALM (Parisi et al., 2022), but distinguishes itself by being applicable to general-purpose settings rather than just task-specific finetuning.

sections_summary.summary: Outlines the limitations of current LMs (hallucinations, lack of up-to-date info, poor math skills) and proposes Toolformer as a self-supervised solution for tool use.
Describes the three-step process: sampling API calls using in-context learning, filtering them based on loss reduction, and finetuning the model on the augmented dataset.
Details the five tools used: Question Answering (Atlas), Calculator, Wikipedia Search (BM25), Machine Translation (NLLB), and a Calendar.
Presents results across LAMA, math, QA, multilingual, and temporal benchmarks, showing Toolformer's superior zero-shot performance compared to baselines.
Investigates the effect of decoding strategies (k-value) and provides a qualitative analysis of data quality.
Discusses prior work on language model pretraining, tool use, and bootstrapping techniques.
Acknowledges limitations such as the inability to chain tools, lack of interactivity, sensitivity to input, and sample inefficiency.

figures_and_tables.what_it_shows: Exemplary predictions of Toolformer using different APIs.

reproducibility: The paper provides detailed information on the training process, prompts, and hyperparameters. It uses publicly available models (GPT-J, Atlas, NLLB) and datasets (CCNet, LAMA, MLQA, etc.). Code and data are implied to be available or reproducible via the provided descriptions.
